item.title: Jakarta EE vs EJB vs Spring: Clarifying Java Enterprise Development
item.description:
“Jakarta EE vs EJB vs Spring: Clarifying Java Enterprise Development”

FAQs on Jakarta EE vs EJB vs Spring

Q: What is Jakarta EE and how has its naming evolved

ANS: Jakarta EE, formerly known as Java EE, is an umbrella specification for developing component-based, multi-tier enterprise applications. The name change from Java EE to Jakarta EE began with version 8 in September 2019. Historically, “J2EE” referred to versions 1.2 through 1.4, while “Java EE” covered versions 5 through 8. You can find more details on its history on Wikipedia’s Jakarta EE page .

Q: Is Jakarta EE only a specification or are there implementations

ANS: Jakarta EE is fundamentally an abstract specification, meaning it defines a set of APIs and technologies that developers can use. The actual working implementations of these specifications are provided by application servers. Examples of full Jakarta EE application servers include WildFly, TomEE, GlassFish, Liberty, and WebLogic. Simpler servlet containers like Tomcat and Jetty implement only a subset of the Jakarta EE APIs, primarily JSP/Servlet functionalities. Developers should code against the specification (importing jakarta.* classes) to ensure their applications are portable across different implementations, similar to how JDBC drivers function. For a basic understanding of related concepts, see What is a factory? .

Q: Is EJB a part of Jakarta EE

ANS: Yes, EJB (Enterprise JavaBeans) is a component architecture and a vital part of the Jakarta EE specification. Full Jakarta EE application servers include support for EJB out-of-the-box, whereas basic servlet containers typically do not. For those starting with Java/Jakarta EE web development, resources like Java / Jakarta EE web development, where do I start and what skills do I need? can be beneficial.

Q: How does Spring relate to EJB and Jakarta EE

ANS: Spring is a standalone framework and a competitor to Jakarta EE. It offers an alternative and often enhanced approach to many Jakarta EE features. For instance, Spring MVC competes with Faces/REST/MVC, Spring DI/IoC/AOP competes with CDI, and Spring Security competes with JASPIC/Security. Spring applications generally do not require a full Jakarta EE environment and can run on simpler environments like Tomcat.
